situations.title: Flight cancelled
situations.owed: A full refund of the unused ticket, including taxes and fees, to your original form of payment, if you do not accept a rebooking, travel credit, voucher or miles. It does not matter why the flight was cancelled or whether the ticket was non-refundable.
situations.when: Automatically, without a request, within 7 business days for credit card purchases and 20 calendar days for cash or other payments, once the airline knows you are not taking the alternative it offered.
situations.detail: Applies to every airline flying to, from or within the US. If you accept the rebooked flight or a voucher, no ticket refund is owed; a voucher offered instead of a refund must be valid for at least 5 years.
steps: Decline the rebooking, voucher or miles if you want your money back.
Reply to the airline's notice or cancel the booking and ask for a refund to your original payment method.
If a travel agency charged your card, the agency is the one that must refund the fare.
If the refund does not arrive on time, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Big delay or schedule change
situations.owed: A full refund of the unused ticket if you choose not to fly the changed itinerary and decline rebooking, credit or other compensation.
situations.when: Automatically, within 7 business days for credit card purchases and 20 calendar days for other payments, after you reject the airline's offer or the changed flight departs without you.
situations.detail: DOT counts a change as significant when a domestic flight departs or arrives 3 hours or more off the original schedule, an international flight 6 hours or more, the departure or arrival airport changes, connections are added, you are downgraded to a lower class, or a passenger with a disability loses a needed accessibility feature or connecting airport. If you fly the changed or delayed flight, no ticket refund is owed.
steps: Compare the new times with the schedule you bought; the 3-hour and 6-hour tests use the original times.
Tell the airline before the deadline it sets that you do not accept the new itinerary.
Ask for the refund to your original form of payment, not a voucher.
If the airline refuses or pays late, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Checked bag delayed
situations.owed: A refund of the fee you paid to check the bag.
situations.when: Due once the bag is not delivered within 12 hours of a domestic flight's arrival, or within 15 hours for international flights of 12 hours or less and 30 hours for longer international flights; paid within 7 business days for card purchases or 20 calendar days for other payments.
situations.detail: You must file a mishandled baggage report with the airline to get the fee back; the fee is also refundable if the airline declares the bag lost. Reasonable expenses while you wait for the bag are a separate claim to the airline.
steps: File a mishandled baggage report with the airline as soon as you learn the bag did not arrive, and keep the report number.
Note the time you were able to leave the plane and the time you got the bag.
If the fee is not refunded automatically, ask the airline in writing.
If it refuses, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Paid extra not provided
situations.owed: A refund of the fee for any paid extra you did not get, such as Wi-Fi, seat selection, checked or carry-on bags, in-flight entertainment, meals or lounge access.
situations.when: Automatically, within 7 business days for credit card purchases and 20 calendar days for other payments, from the time the airline knows the service was not provided.
situations.detail: Applies when the service was unavailable through no fault of yours, for example broken Wi-Fi, a cancelled flight or being bumped. Ask the airline, not the travel agency, for these refunds.
steps: Keep proof of the purchase and of the service not being provided, such as a receipt or a note from the crew.
If the refund is not issued automatically, ask the airline for it through its refund form.
If it refuses, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Downgraded to a lower class
situations.owed: The difference between the fare you paid and the fare for the lower class you actually flew. If you decide not to travel because of the downgrade, a full refund of the unused ticket instead.
situations.when: Within 7 business days for credit card purchases and 20 calendar days for other payments.
situations.detail: An involuntary downgrade counts as a significant change under DOT rules. If you are moved to a lower class because the flight is overbooked, the fare difference replaces denied boarding compensation.
steps: Keep your original boarding pass and the one for the seat you actually used.
Ask the airline for the fare difference through its refund form.
If it refuses, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Airline-caused delay or cancellation
situations.owed: Rebooking on the same airline at no extra cost, a meal or meal voucher when you wait 3 hours or more, and a hotel with ground transportation for an overnight wait, if your airline has committed to them. These are commitments shown airline by airline on the DOT dashboard, not a federal rule, and no listed airline commits to cash compensation.
situations.when: Meal commitments apply once a controllable cancellation or delay has you waiting 3 hours or more; hotel and transport commitments apply to overnight disruptions. Check your airline's column on the dashboard before you ask.
situations.detail: Controllable means caused by the airline, such as maintenance or crew problems, cabin cleaning, baggage loading or fueling; weather and air traffic control delays are not covered. Not every airline commits to every item, and DOT holds airlines to what their customer service plans promise.
steps: Look up your airline on the DOT dashboard to see what it promises.
Ask airline staff at the airport for the meal voucher, hotel and transport.
If you have to pay yourself, keep receipts and ask the airline for reimbursement afterwards.
If the airline does not honor a commitment, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Bumped from an overbooked flight
situations.owed: Cash compensation if you are bumped involuntarily and arrive more than 1 hour late: 200% of your one-way fare, up to $1,075, for a domestic arrival delay of 1 to 2 hours or an international delay of 1 to 4 hours, and 400%, up to $2,150, for longer delays. You also keep the right to a refund of the unused ticket.
situations.when: At the airport on the same day, by cash or check; within 24 hours if the airline puts you on a flight that leaves before it can pay you. You may refuse a voucher and insist on the cash amount.
situations.detail: You must have checked in by the deadline and be at the gate on time. No compensation if the airline gets you there within 1 hour of the original arrival, or if the bump is due to a smaller aircraft, weight and balance limits on planes with 60 or fewer seats, a downgrade (you get the fare difference instead), a charter, a plane with fewer than 30 seats, or an international flight departing from a foreign country.
steps: Do not volunteer unless the offer suits you; ask whether you are at risk of being bumped involuntarily.
If bumped, ask for the written statement of your rights that the airline must give you.
Ask for payment by cash or check before you leave the airport and keep your boarding pass.
If the airline refuses, file a DOT complaint.

situations.title: Airline refuses the refund
situations.owed: A complaint with the US DOT Office of Aviation Consumer Protection. DOT forwards it to the airline, which must answer you and DOT, and DOT can take enforcement action.
situations.when: Give the airline a chance first; airlines must acknowledge a written complaint within 30 days and send a written response within 60 days. Then file with DOT.
situations.detail: Covers airlines flying to, from or within the US and ticket agents. Safety and security concerns go to the FAA and TSA instead.
steps: Write to the airline's customer relations office first and keep a copy.
If the answer is late or unsatisfactory, file the DOT online complaint with your flight details and documents.
The airline must respond to you and to DOT; DOT reviews the case for violations.

situations.title: Flight cancelled (EU)
situations.owed: A choice between a refund of the unused ticket (plus a flight back to your starting point if you are mid-journey) and re-routing, care at the airport, and fixed compensation of EUR 250 (1,500 km or less), EUR 400 (over 1,500 km within the EU, or 1,500 to 3,500 km elsewhere) or EUR 600 (over 3,500 km).
situations.when: Compensation is due if you were told less than 14 days before departure, unless the re-routing gets you there close to the original times or the airline proves extraordinary circumstances such as severe weather or air traffic control decisions. Refunds must be paid within 7 days.
situations.detail: Covers flights departing an EU airport on any airline, flights arriving in the EU on an EU airline, and flights to or from Iceland, Norway and Switzerland. Technical problems found in routine maintenance and the airline's own staff strikes do not count as extraordinary.
steps: Ask the airline for meals, drinks, a hotel if you must stay overnight and transport to it; keep receipts if you pay yourself.
Choose a refund or re-routing, then claim compensation from the airline in writing.
If the airline does not answer within 2 months or rejects you, complain to the national enforcement body of the country where it happened.
Alternative dispute resolution or the European Small Claims procedure are further options.

situations.title: Flight delayed 3 hours or more (EU)
situations.owed: Fixed compensation of EUR 250, EUR 400 or EUR 600 depending on the flight distance if you reach your final destination 3 hours or more late, plus meals and drinks while you wait and a hotel if the delay runs overnight.
situations.when: Care starts after a departure delay of 2 hours (1,500 km or less), 3 hours (1,500 to 3,500 km) or 4 hours (longer flights). At 5 hours you may give up the trip and get a refund within 7 days. Compensation is not due if the airline proves extraordinary circumstances.
situations.detail: Covers flights departing an EU airport on any airline, flights arriving in the EU on an EU airline, and flights to or from Iceland, Norway and Switzerland. The delay that counts is at the final destination on your booking, including a missed connection on the same ticket.
steps: Ask airline staff for food, drink and, if needed, a hotel; keep receipts if you pay yourself.
Note your actual arrival time at the final destination.
Claim compensation from the airline first, in writing.
No reply in 2 months or a refusal: complain to the national enforcement body of the country where the delay happened.

situations.title: Flight cancelled (UK)
situations.owed: A choice between a refund of the unused parts of your ticket and an alternative flight, care while you wait, and compensation of GBP 220 (under 1,500 km), GBP 350 (1,500 to 3,500 km) or GBP 520 (over 3,500 km) if you were told less than 14 days before departure.
situations.when: Compensation depends on the notice you got and how late the replacement flight gets you there: with 7 to 14 days' notice it is halved (GBP 110, 175 or 260) when the replacement arrives within set limits, and it is not due at all if the cancellation was caused by extraordinary circumstances.
situations.detail: UK261 covers flights departing a UK airport on any airline, flights arriving at a UK airport on a UK or EU airline, and flights arriving at an EU airport on a UK airline. If a connection is cancelled mid-journey, you can also get a flight back to your starting point.
steps: Decide between a refund and an alternative flight; the airline must offer both.
Ask for food, drink, a hotel and transport if you have to wait, and keep receipts.
Claim compensation from the airline in writing if you had less than 14 days' notice.
If rejected or no final answer in 8 weeks, use the airline's ADR scheme or the CAA's Passenger Advice and Complaints Team.

actions.label: CAA: how to make a complaint

situations.title: Flight delayed 3 hours or more (UK)
situations.owed: Food and drink while you wait, a hotel if the delay runs overnight, and fixed compensation if you arrive at your destination more than 3 hours late: GBP 220 (under 1,500 km), GBP 350 (1,500 to 3,500 km) or GBP 520 (over 3,500 km; GBP 260 if you arrive 3 to 4 hours late).
situations.when: Care starts after a delay of 2 hours (under 1,500 km), 3 hours (1,500 to 3,500 km) or 4 hours (over 3,500 km). At 5 hours you can choose not to travel and get a refund. Compensation is not automatic; claim it from the airline, and escalate if there is no final answer within 8 weeks.
situations.detail: UK261 covers flights departing a UK airport on any airline, flights arriving at a UK airport on a UK or EU airline, and flights arriving at an EU airport on a UK airline. No compensation if the delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances such as extreme weather or air traffic control strikes.
steps: Ask airline staff for food and drink vouchers and a hotel if needed; keep itemised receipts if you pay yourself.
Claim compensation and expenses from the airline in writing, following its claims procedure.
If the airline rejects the claim or takes more than 8 weeks, go to its ADR scheme (AviationADR or CEDR) or, if it has none, the CAA's Passenger Advice and Complaints Team.
